1: Good afternoon. My name is Lanqing Luo. This thesis investigates how one RGB-D camera and a kinematic model can reconstruct a person handling an object with both hands, without wearable sensors or a motion-capture laboratory.
2: I will follow three blocks. First, motivation and goal. Second, the offline reconstruction system, starting with its architecture and then each module. Third, results and next steps, including the move to real-time reconstruction, limitations and future directions.
3: Body and object reconstruction supports applications such as robot demonstrations and avatar animation. The methods reviewed here use different sensing arrangements. Wearables place hardware on the user, while bimanual capture datasets often require camera rigs. The selected RGB-D methods track hands or body landmarks; monocular methods can reconstruct two hands but leave depth ambiguous. Our goal is to reconstruct the upper body and a handled object together in one metric scene, using one RGB-D camera.
4: The setup uses one RealSense D435, three printed ArUco markers and a connected body model. Nothing is worn on the person. The output places the upper body and cube in the same calibrated Unity scene. The recording shows the task we want to reconstruct: carrying the cube, placing it on a rail and transferring it between hands.
5: Here is the complete offline system. Capture provides aligned colour and depth. In the person branch, MediaPipe detects landmarks, depth supplies their third coordinate, and preprocessing cleans their tracks. Recovery supplies supported missing points before the kinematic solver calculates thirteen angles. In the scene branch, static markers establish the reference frame and the moving marker tracks the cube. Its pose can also support body recovery. Timestamped outputs then meet in Unity. I will explain the modules first and return to this layout for integration.
6: The raw observations have three recurring problems: spikes, short gaps and jitter. We address them in that order, with Hampel rejection, linear interpolation and Butterworth smoothing. Each operation has a separate role.
7: MediaPipe reports thirty-three landmarks. We retain eight: the shoulder, elbow, wrist and hip pairs. At each image location, a five-by-five depth median supplies the third coordinate. Low visibility or missing depth makes the observation unavailable. The overlay shows the detector output before the three cleaning steps.
8: First, spikes. The Hampel filter compares each sample with the median of a centred seven-frame window. The threshold is three times the scaled median absolute deviation, with a two-centimetre floor. A sample outside that threshold is rejected and marked missing, ready for the next stage.
9: Second, short gaps. For an interior gap of at most five frames, we interpolate between the accepted samples on either side. The equation gives a straight line in time. Filled samples keep a repair flag, and longer gaps remain open for the recovery layer.
10: Third, jitter. A fourth-order Butterworth low-pass filter at three hertz smooths the small fluctuations. Running it forward and backward removes phase delay. The backward pass uses future samples, so this operation belongs to the offline system. We will replace it in the causal version.
11: How do we turn these separate points into a connected body? The model has three levels: a torso root at L24, shoulders carried by that root, and elbows carried by the shoulders. First I will show the chain, then explain the construction of each local frame.
12: The eight landmarks form a chain from the right hip, L24, through the torso and shoulders to the elbows and wrists. Each local frame moves with its parent. This structure lets us use segment lengths and joint relationships consistently. The T-pose provides the reference: the arm angles are zero and the local frames are aligned. We construct the model in the y-up camera frame; the reason for its handedness is covered in the backup pages.
13: At the root, L24 is the origin. The hip line, from left hip to right hip, defines x. The direction towards the right shoulder provides an upward reference; removing its component along x gives the orthogonal y direction. The cross product completes z. These three unit axes form the rotation matrix, and the hip position supplies the translation. Together they describe the root frame relative to the camera frame.
14: At the shoulder, swing points the upper arm using an azimuth and an elevation. Twist rotates around the upper arm itself. To obtain twist, we express the forearm after undoing the swing. A straight arm leaves this rotation unobservable because the forearm lies along the same axis. The system therefore holds the previous twist until the elbow bends and provides that information again.
15: The shoulder rotation carries the elbow frame down the upper arm. We express the wrist-to-elbow direction in that local frame, separating elbow movement from torso and shoulder movement. The equation extracts two angular coordinates; the video highlights flexion. The model outputs three root angles, three at each shoulder and two at each elbow, giving thirteen angles in total.
16: Object tracking starts with a fixed camera and environment. This gives us two marker roles: static markers define the scene, and a dynamic marker follows the cube.
17: The desk marker defines the World origin and anchors the Unity scene. The wall marker supplies an environmental vertical reference. For each static marker, we average the first ten valid detections. Positions use an arithmetic mean; the averaged orientation is projected back onto a proper rotation. Both branches then use this fixed calibration.
18: The cube marker is tracked in every frame. Combining its camera pose with the calibrated camera-to-World transformation puts the object in the desk reference. The track accepts a sample when detection succeeds, the pose is finite and the displacement remains within the allowed motion bounds. Those bounds grow with the time since the last accepted sample. The result is a cleaned object track in World coordinates.
19: Partial occlusion is one module of the reconstruction system. It first identifies unreliable observations, then uses three forms of support: direction memory for a missing wrist, the object for a grasping wrist, and two-link geometry for a missing elbow. A joint group without enough support holds its last valid angles. Let us start with the reliability checks.
20: This stage has three parts: six detectors, wrong to missing, and three output states. The detectors check acquisition validity, segment length, hip-shoulder alignment, shoulder-to-hip width ratio, landmark displacement, and grasp plausibility. A rejected observation becomes missing, so it cannot distort the solve. For a flagged arm, the elbow and wrist observations are removed together. Reconstruction then uses the reliable information that remains. Finally, each output group is labelled measured, constrained or held. These labels distinguish direct measurement, supported recovery and the last valid pose.
21: Case A has a missing wrist but a reliable elbow. On measured frames, the forearm direction updates a memory with gain zero point three. During wrist loss, the system places the wrist one calibrated forearm length from the elbow along that remembered direction. This support lasts for up to forty-five consecutive frames, and the reconstructed output is labelled constrained.
22: Case B uses a tracked object to recover a grasping wrist. During a stable grasp, the wrist has an approximately fixed offset in the marker's local frame. Clean observations update that offset slowly. When the wrist disappears, the offset freezes, and the current object pose places the wrist. This method takes priority over direction memory when its conditions hold. Each new grasp begins a new offset estimate.
23: Case C recovers the elbow. We know the shoulder and a measured or rebuilt wrist. One sphere around the shoulder represents the upper-arm length; another around the wrist represents the forearm length. Their intersection is a circle of possible elbows. We project the remembered upper-arm direction into that circle's plane to select one point. The recorded example applies the same construction to the landmark data.
24: When the available observations cannot support these constructions, the affected group holds its last valid angles. Other groups can continue moving. The system also limits angular changes to fifteen degrees per frame and labels a limited output constrained. Each group therefore carries a measured, constrained or held state into Unity. The red markers in this controlled example identify held groups.
25: We can now connect the modules. This is the same architecture as the initial overview, with data moving through it. The person branch produces thirteen angles and their states. The marker branch provides the object pose and its recovery constraint. Both outputs carry frame identity and session time. Shared records make them available to the merger, which evaluates a common render time and publishes one combined state for Unity. The next pages explain the handoffs and mappings.
26: The camera writes aligned frames into an eight-slot ring. Frame n uses slot n modulo eight. An odd sequence means a write is in progress; an even sequence means the slot is settled. Each reader selects the newest settled frame, copies it and checks the sequence again. Matching even values allow acceptance; a changed sequence requires a retry. Here, the slower reader skips frames five twenty-nine through five thirty-two to take five thirty-three. Later, the writer wraps around and overwrites old slots. Skipping an available old frame and overwriting a slot are separate events. The writer does not wait for either reader.
27: The person record is eighty-four bytes, the object record forty-four, and the combined record one hundred and twelve. Each includes a frame index and session time. Recovery rejects object support more than three frames away from the body frame. The merger works two frame intervals behind capture. It interpolates short gaps, holds across longer gaps and blends the return of data over two ticks. This produces a common display time even when the branches finish at different moments.
28: Body data leaves the model in the y-up camera frame. Its mapping into Unity combines the camera-axis conversion, calibrated camera pose and display-axis mapping into one fixed anchor. We compute that anchor once. For each bone, Unity combines the anchor with the solved chain rotation and the bone's captured rest orientation. The rest orientation accounts for the avatar's own local bone axes. Positions pass through the same anchor as points.
29: The ArUco branch uses the right-handed World frame. The matrix S exchanges its second and third coordinates for Unity. A point requires one mapping; an orientation changes both its input and output bases, giving S R S. The wall reference supplies the gravity alignment, and the floor is placed seventy-one point six centimetres below the desk reference. Applying this common scene placement keeps the body and object in the same coordinate system.
30: Here is the integrated reconstruction. The recorded image and Unity display the same source frame. The replay applies the saved pelvis position, thirteen body angles and object pose. It also retains the reconstruction states, so the displayed motion can be interpreted alongside the decisions that produced it. We now evaluate that output.
31: The results have three parts: object reconstruction, body reconstruction without occlusion, and body reconstruction under occlusion. Each comparison uses a stated reference, which I will identify before presenting its measurements.
32: For the object, four waypoints define three tape-measured separations: twenty-five point five, three point five, and thirty-seven point five centimetres. The reconstructed separations differ by zero point five three to two point eight three centimetres across the rail and handover recordings. These are endpoint-distance errors. The carry segment reconstructs slightly short, while the lift and slide reconstruct slightly long.
33: For the unoccluded body, the reference is the accepted raw landmark at the same frame. The model's median wrist error is zero point eight three centimetres on the right and two point three four on the left. After avatar mapping, rendered-joint errors range from five point three to six point eight centimetres. A separate grasp check compares wrist-to-marker distance: the reconstruction gives fifteen point seven seven centimetres on the right and fourteen point zero eight on the left, against a physical distance of about sixteen centimetres.
34: This controlled test removes the right elbow and wrist in three forty-five-frame windows with different motion levels. The torso and shoulder remain available. The reference is the unmasked reconstruction of those same frames. Hold-last, direction memory and object assistance give median wrist and elbow deviations between zero point three and two point five centimetres. Their relative performance changes with the joint, motion and available support.
35: For natural tracking failures, watch and bracelet features provide manual wrist labels. On the right, the median distance to the label changes from eleven point four to five point two centimetres across four frames. On the left, it changes from twelve point three to thirteen point one across sixteen frames. These outcomes show that object assistance depends on the actual grasp and offset conditions. The examples show the two hands separately.
36: The offline system gives us repeatable material for evaluation and can use future samples to bridge gaps and smooth motion. Applications such as motion capture and VR also need output as data arrives. Six operations therefore receive causal replacements: the centred window becomes trailing, Butterworth becomes One Euro, and gap filling uses the merger's delay. Grasp initialisation, grasp exit and object cleaning also update from available observations. The kinematic model stays the same. The trade-off is reconstruction quality against delay.
37: The One Euro filter adapts its cutoff to movement speed: stronger smoothing during slow motion, faster response during movement. In the reported causal replay, the pipeline follows approximately twenty-nine frames per second for nine hundred frames without dropping a frame. The ninety-ninth-percentile processing times are thirteen milliseconds for the body branch and sixteen point seven for the marker branch, within the frame interval. These are branch processing times, distinct from sensor-to-screen latency.
38: On the left is the recorded RGB; on the right is its causal Unity reconstruction. Each RGB frame is paired with the latest available reconstruction state at that time. The oblique view shows the table in front of the person and the wall behind the task. Both remain fixed while the body and cube move. This demonstration uses the calibrated scene and the recorded causal outputs.
39: The present evaluation covers one subject and three slow recordings. Object accuracy uses endpoint separations; a registered physical trajectory would support a fuller path comparison. Body dimensions are estimated from landmarks, and recovery outcomes vary with the hand and grasp. The causal pipeline was evaluated using recorded replay; direct live-sensor operation remains a further validation step. These points define where the evaluation can be extended.
40: One useful extension is to retain reliable image pixels when depth fails. The current rejection discards the complete landmark, although its two-dimensional location may still be useful, as the Waterloo work motivates. Dong and Payandeh's Bayesian kinematic approach suggests how uncertain observations can be combined with a connected model. We could use valid pixels, available depth and our kinematic constraints together to estimate hidden joints. Broader testing, additional calibrated views and stronger detection are further directions.
41: This thesis demonstrates upper-body and object reconstruction in one calibrated scene using a single RGB-D camera. The connected model and object constraints support recovery during local observation failures, with explicit output states. A causal implementation processes recorded data within the frame budget. The system provides a basis for broader evaluation and reconstruction that makes better use of partial observations.
